an1.278:1.1: A wheel-turning monarch established dominion over the entire land from ocean to ocean ([dn17](), [dn26]()).
an1.279:1.1: This section asserts that a women cannot fulfill the roles of foremost leadership, whether spiritual (Buddha), earthly (wheel-turning monarch), or heavenly (Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā). The Buddha lived in a patriarchal society where female leadership at this level was unknown, and it is perhaps assumed that people would not follow a woman in that role; a similar argument is made today for why a woman should not be chosen as Presidential candidate. Similar reasoning may be behind the idea that a Buddha is born either an aristocrat or a brahmin, whichever is the leading class of the time ([dn14:1.5.1]()). Still, this does not explain why such a statement would be made. It is of no spiritual relevance, since a woman may realize full liberation as an arahant in this very life. It cannot be about a woman making a vow to be a Buddha in the future, as no such vow is found anywhere in early Buddhism. It is also hard to understand how this knowledge can be a form of insight, since it depends on social structures and customary beliefs that arose in particular historical conditions. The Chinese parallel of the Bahudhātukasutta at MA 181 lacks this passage entirely, while other parallels exhibit inconsistencies and a tendency to growth over time (Anālayo, “The Bahudhātuka-sutta and its Parallels”, Journal of Buddhist Ethics, vol 16, 2009). Most likely these passages were added at a time when female leadership in the Saṅgha was contested, for which see [an8.51]() and notes.
an1.281-283:1.1: While we encounter these divinities as individuals, they are understood as being stations or offices in the leading role of their particular realms. Thus, for example, Moggallāna said that he used to be Māra in a past life ([mn50:8.1]()).
